s: A company wants to use AWS for disaster recovery for an on-premises application. The company has hundreds of Windows-based servers that run the application. All the servers mount a common share. The company has an RTO of 15 minutes and an RPO of 5 minutes. The solution must support native failover and fallback capabilities. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
o: Create an AWS Storage Gateway File Gateway. Schedule daily Windows server backups. Save the data lo Amazon S3. During a disaster, recover the on-premises servers from the backup. During failback. run the on-premises servers on Amazon EC2 instances.

Create a set of AWS CloudFormation templates to create infrastructure. Replicate all data to Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) by using AWS DataSync. During a disaster, use AWS CodePipeline to deploy the templates to restore the on-premises servers. Fail back the data by using DataSync.

Create an AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) pipeline to stand up a multi-site active-active environment on AWS. Replicate data into Amazon S3 by using the s3 sync command. During a disaster, swap DNS endpoints to point to AWS. Fail back the data by using the s3 sync command.

Use AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery to replicate the on-premises servers. Replicate data to an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file system by using AWS DataSync. Mount the file system to AWS servers. During a disaster, fail over the on-premises servers to AWS. Fail back to new or existing servers by using Elastic Disaster Recovery.
e: For cost-effective disaster recovery with 15-minute RTO and 5-minute RPO for hundreds of Windows servers: l AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS): Provides continuous replication with RPO of seconds and RTO of minutes. It automatically maintains low-cost recovery instances in AWS and supports rapid failover. It's designed specifically for this DR use case and includes native failover/fallback capabilities. l Alternative: CloudEndure Disaster Recovery: Also provides continuous replication and supports failover/fallback, though DRS is the newer AWS-native service These solutions meet the RTO/RPO requirements and provide native failover capabilities. Cheaper alternatives like periodic backups alone wouldn't achieve the 5-minute RPO. Shared storage replication to AWS FSx would be complex and expensive for this scenario.

w.y: RTO 15 minutes, RPO 5 minutes, and native failover and failback for hundreds of servers point to AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery. FSx for Windows File Server holds the shared SMB data, kept in sync with DataSync.

o.A: Daily backups give an RPO of a day and a long restore.
o.B: Rebuilding servers from templates during a disaster cannot meet a 15-minute RTO.
o.C: An active-active copy is the most expensive option, and s3 sync is not a file share.
o.D: Correct: Elastic Disaster Recovery for servers, FSx for Windows for the share, built-in failback.
